findings.claim: Removing the `try`/`finally` means `this.writer` is never re-acquired when `body.pipeTo(...)` rejects, leaving the StreamingApi permanently without a writer (the writable stays unlocked/errored and `this.writer` still refers to the released writer).
findings.rationale: `this.writer.releaseLock()` is called unconditionally before the pipe. Previously the `finally` block guaranteed `this.writer = this.writable.getWriter()` ran even if `pipeTo` threw (aborted request, source stream error, client disconnect). Now any rejection propagates out of `pipe()` and skips the re-acquire, so any later `write()`/`close()` on the instance will throw `TypeError: Invalid state: The writer is released`, or the object is left in an inconsistent half-piped state. Callers that catch the pipe error and try to continue writing (a common pattern for streaming handlers) will break. High confidence this is a real regression.

findings.claim: Dropping `preventAbort: true` changes error semantics: an error in the source `body` now aborts the destination `this.writable` (the whole response stream) instead of leaving it intact.
findings.rationale: With `preventAbort` unset (default false), `pipeTo` forwards source errors by calling `writable.abort()`, which errors the underlying response stream so nothing further can be written or gracefully closed. Combined with the removed `finally`, `this.writable.getWriter()` on an aborted stream would also yield an errored writer. This is a behavior change for existing callers that relied on the pipe failing in isolation; moderate-to-high confidence it is unintentional since `preventClose` was kept.
